label: main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{main}
For every block graph $G$,
\[
\mathrm{CFD}(G)=\mathrm{LGD}(G)=\mathrm{LFD}(G).
\]
Moreover, an optimal set $D$ of edges to delete, together with a forest $R$ such that $G-D\cong L(R)$, can be computed in $O(n+m)$ time.
head: environment

label: lem1
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose $u_iu_j$ were an edge for some $i\neq j$.
Then the three edges $vu_i$, $vu_j$ and $u_iu_j$ form a triangle, and a triangle lies inside a single block.
This would put $B_i$ and $B_j$ in the same block, contradicting that they are distinct. \qed

label: completion
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{completion}
Let $G$ be a block graph and let $H$ be any claw-free spanning subgraph of $G$.
For every block $B\in\mathcal{B}$ let
\[
S_B=\{v\in B : \text{ there exists an edge of $H$ incident to $v$ that lies in } B\},
\]
and let $J$ be the graph on $V(G)$ obtained from $H$ by adding all the edges inside  $S_B$ for all $B \in \mathcal{B}$.
Then $H\subseteq J\subseteq G$, the graph $J$ is claw-free, and every vertex of $G$ belongs to at most two of the sets $S_B$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
An edge of $H$ lies in a unique block $B$, and both of its endpoints belong to $S_B$, so $H\subseteq J$.
Every block of $G$ is a clique, so every pair inside $S_B\subseteq B$ is an edge of $G$, which gives $J\subseteq G$.

We now show that no vertex $v$ lies in three of the sets, say $S_{B_1}$, $S_{B_2}$ and $S_{B_3}$ for three distinct blocks.
For each $i$, since $v\in S_{B_i}$, there is a neighbour $u_i\in B_i\setminus\{v\}$ with $vu_i\in E(H)$.
By \Cref{lem1} the vertices $u_1,u_2,u_3$ are pairwise nonadjacent in $G$, hence also in $H$.
Together with $v$ they form an induced claw in $H$, a contradiction.
So every vertex belongs to at most two of the sets $S_B$.

Finally, we show that $J$ is claw-free.
The neighbours of a vertex $v$ in $J$ are the vertices of the sets $S_B$ that contain $v$, other than $v$ itself.
There are at most two such sets, and each is a clique in $J$.
So the neighbourhood of $v$ is the union of at most two cliques, and it cannot contain three pairwise nonadjacent vertices. \qed
head: environment

label: lem3
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem3}
Let $S_B\subseteq B$ be a set for every block $B\in\mathcal{B}$ such that every vertex lies in at most two of the sets $S_B$.
Let $J_S$ be the graph on $V(G)$ with edge set $\bigcup_{B}\binom{S_B}{2}$.
Then $J_S$ is the line graph of a forest $R$, and $R$ can be built in $O(n)$ time from the sets $S_B$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We can getrid of all sets $S_B$ of size at most one, since they contribute no edges to $J_S$. In the rest of the construction, membership always refers to these retained sets. For each retained $S_B$, create a vertex $r_B$ of $R$.
For every vertex $v$ of $G$ create an edge $e_v$ of $R$ as follows.
If $v$ lies in two sets $S_B$ and $S_C$, let $e_v=r_Br_C$.
If $v$ lies in exactly one set $S_B$, let $e_v$ join $r_B$ to a new private leaf.
If $v$ lies in no set, let $e_v$ be a new edge on two new vertices, disjoint from other vertices of $R$.

No two of these edges are parallel. If $e_u$ and $e_v$ both joined $r_B$ and $r_C$, then $u,v\in B\cap C$, but distinct blocks share at most one vertex. Any cycle in $R$ would use only vertices $r_B$, since all other vertices are private endpoints. A cycle $r_{B_1}r_{B_2}\cdots r_{B_k}$ in $R$ would give an incidence cycle $B_1v_1B_2v_2\cdots B_kv_k$ in $T$, which is a forest. Hence $R$ is a forest.

For every vertex \(v\in V(G)\), the construction creates a unique edge \(e_v\in E(R)\). Hence the map
$$
\phi:V(J_S)\longrightarrow E(R),\qquad \phi(v)=e_v,
$$
is a bijection. It remains to show that $\phi$ preserves adjacency. By definition, $u,v\in V(G)$ are adjacent in $J_S$ if and only if they lie in some retained $S_B$. Every vertex of such an $S_B$ corresponds to an edge incident with $r_B$ and private endpoints are never shared. Thus $u,v\in S_B$ for some retained block if and only if $e_u$ and $e_v$ share an endpoint, or equivalently $e_ue_v\in E(L(R))$. Hence
$$
uv\in E(J_S)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
e_ue_v\in E(L(R)),
$$
and therefore \(J_S\cong L(R)\).

The construction of $R$ takes $O(n)$ time. Since every vertex belongs to at most two original sets $S_B$, we have
$$\sum_{B\in\mathcal B}|S_B|\le 2n.$$
We go through the sets and discard those of size at most one, create $r_B$ for each retained set, and record only retained memberships for each vertex $v$. This takes $O(n)$ time. Processing each vertex once then creates $e_v$ in constant time from its zero, one, or two retained memberships. Hence $R$ has exactly $n$ edges and $O(n)$ vertices.

title: Definition
body_md: A \emph{selection} is a family $S=(S_B)_{B\in\mathcal{B}}$ of sets $S_B\subseteq B$ such that every vertex of $G$ lies in at most two of the sets $S_B$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Take an optimal selection $S$.
By \Cref{lem3} the graph $J_S$ is the line graph of a forest, and it is a spanning subgraph of $G$ with $\mathrm{OPT}(G)$ edges.
Deleting the other $m-\mathrm{OPT}(G)$ edges of $G$ therefore gives a line graph of a forest, so $\mathrm{LFD}(G)\le m-\mathrm{OPT}(G)$.

Conversely, let $H$ be any claw-free spanning subgraph of $G$.
By \Cref{completion} the sets $S_B$ form a selection, and $H\subseteq J$, so
\[
|E(H)|\le |E(J)|=\sum_{B}\binom{|S_B|}{2}\le\mathrm{OPT}(G).
\]
So every claw-free solution deletes at least $m-\mathrm{OPT}(G)$ edges, that is, $\mathrm{CFD}(G)\ge m-\mathrm{OPT}(G)$.

Putting these inequalities together with the general inequality in \Cref{ineq} we get
\[
\mathrm{LFD}(G)\le m-\mathrm{OPT}(G)\le\mathrm{CFD}(G)\le\mathrm{LGD}(G)\le\mathrm{LFD}(G),
\]
so all these numbers are equal.
head: environment

label: cor:diamond
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:diamond}
Let $\mathrm{CDFD}(G)$ be the minimum number of edges whose deletion makes $G$ both claw-free and diamond-free, where a diamond is $K_4$ minus one edge. For every block graph $G$,
\[
\mathrm{CDFD}(G)=\mathrm{CFD}(G)=\mathrm{LGD}(G)=\mathrm{LFD}(G)=m-\mathrm{OPT}(G).
\]
An optimal deletion set can be found in $O(n+m)$ time.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Clearly $\mathrm{CFD}(G)\leq\mathrm{CDFD}(G)$. For any two forest edges meeting at $x$, an edge adjacent to both must also meet at $x$, since otherwise those three edges form a cycle. Thus the common neighbors of an adjacent pair in the line graph form a clique, as a result there are no induced diamond. Therefore, the line graph of a forest is claw-free and diamond-free. 

Hence $\mathrm{CDFD}(G)\leq\mathrm{LFD}(G)$, and \Cref{same_ineq} gives the equality. The algorithm in \Cref{sec:dp,sec:linear} returns the corresponding set.
head: environment

label: dp_prop
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{dp_prop}
If the values $D_v(x)$ and $M_B(x)$ are computed from the leaves of the rooted block-vertex forest upward using the recurrences above, then for each component with root $r$, the value $D_r(0)$ is the maximum number of edges that can be kept in that component. Consequently,
$$
\mathrm{OPT}(G)=\sum_r D_r(0),
$$
where the sum is over the roots of all components of the block-vertex forest.

Moreover, if we store the choices attaining the maxima in the recurrences, then an optimal selection can be recovered by tracing these choices from the roots downward.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We argue by induction from the leaves of the rooted block-vertex forest.

Suppose first that the current node is a vertex $v$. Once we decide in which child blocks $v$ is chosen, the subtrees rooted at those child blocks are independent. The only restriction linking them is that $v$ can be chosen in at most $2-x$ child blocks when its state is $x$. Hence the best value is obtained by using the available slots on the child blocks with the largest gains, which gives~\eqref{eqn5}. Thus $D_v(x)$ is the optimum value for the subtree rooted at $v$.

Now suppose the current node is a block $B$. Once we fix the set $A$ of child vertices chosen in $B$, the subtrees rooted at these children are independent. A chosen child $u$ contributes $D_u(1)$ instead of $D_u(0)$, a loss of $c_u$, while the vertices chosen in $B$ contribute $\binom{|A|+x}{2}$ edges inside the clique $B$. Maximizing over all choices of $A$ therefore gives~\eqref{eqn7}, so $M_B(x)$ is the optimum value for the subtree rooted at $B$.

At a root vertex $r$ no parent block is present, so both slots are free and the optimum for that component is $D_r(0)$. Since different components are independent, their values add, giving

$$
\mathrm{OPT}(G)=\sum_r D_r(0).
$$

Finally, by storing the choices attaining each maximum, an optimal selection can be recovered by tracing the decisions from the roots downward.
head: environment

label: cutoff
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{cutoff}
Let $B$ be a block of size $s$. If a child vertex $v$ of $B$ has cost $c_v\ge s$, then no set attaining the maximum in~\eqref{eqn7} contains $v$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that an optimal set $A$ contains $v$. Remove $v$ from $A$, so it is no longer chosen in the current block $B$. This does not remove $v$ from the graph or its child blocks. Its state changes from $1$ to $0$, so the optimum contribution below $v$ increases from $D_v(1)$ to $D_v(0)$, a gain of $c_v\geq s$.

Inside $B$, removing $v$ from the chosen set loses only the edges joining $v$ to the other chosen vertices of $B$. Since $B$ has $s$ vertices, at most $s-1$ such edges are lost. Hence the total change in the objective is at least
$c_v-(s-1)\ge 1.$

Thus removing $v$ from $A$ strictly improves the solution, contradicting the optimality of $A$.
head: environment

label: thm:stars
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:stars}
For every fixed $r\ge1$, the minimum number of edges whose deletion makes a block graph $K_{1,r+1}$-free can be computed in $O(n+m)$ time.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We follow the proof for $r=2$ and list only what changes.
In a $K_{1,r+1}$-free spanning subgraph $H$, a vertex lies in at most $r$ of the sets $S_B$, since $r+1$ of them would give $r+1$ pairwise nonadjacent neighbors by \Cref{lem1}.
The completed graph $J$ is again $K_{1,r+1}$-free, because the neighbourhood of a vertex is the union of at most $r$ cliques.
Conversely, any family of sets in which every vertex lies in at most $r$ of them gives a $K_{1,r+1}$-free graph in the same way.
So the problem is~\eqref{eqn4} with ``at most two'' replaced by ``at most $r$''.
Pad the child-block gains with zeros and let $g_1(v)\ge\cdots\ge g_r(v)\ge0$ be the $r$ largest values. In state $x\in\{0,1\}$, vertex $v$ has $r-x$ free slots, so
\[
D_v(x)=\sum_{B\in\mathrm{ch}(v)}M_B(0)+\sum_{i=1}^{r-x}g_i(v),
\qquad c_v=D_v(0)-D_v(1)=g_r(v).
\]
The block step~\eqref{eqn7} and \Cref{cutoff} are unchanged, so the grouping method still takes $O(|B|)$ time per block, and for fixed $r$ the $r$ largest gains at a vertex can be kept up to date in $O(r)$ time per child.
Recovering the solution works as before.
